title: Free is wanting rightly
hookLine: the free person lives as they wish, which means wishing rightly
carry: same person, same day, different leash
last: AT HOME HERE — THERE IS WORK FOR YOU TO DO.

cards: Ask what freedom means, and a common answer is: doing what I want. No boss, no curfew, nobody telling me what to do. It's a fine answer.
Epictetus starts a long talk with almost the same definition, then pulls a thread until the whole sweater comes apart. Book four, chapter one, is called On Freedom.
He had a stake in the question: elsewhere in the Discourses he mentions the master he once had.

teach.b: He opens: the free person lives as they wish, and can't be forced, blocked or compelled. Then he pulls.

teach.h: NO ONE WISHES TO LIVE IN ERROR.
teach.b: Does anyone wish to live in error? To be deceived, unjust, frightened, out of control? No one does.
So anyone who lives that way is not living as they wish, and by the first definition, isn't free. Freedom turns out not to be about how many doors are open.
It's about whether what you want is something you can have without betraying yourself.
To make it vivid, he tells of a slave who longs to be freed. Once I'm free, he thinks, everything will be fine. He gets his freedom, and soon needs a patron to flatter for dinner.
He climbs, saves, gets rich, maybe even rises to the senate.
And at every rung he serves someone, chasing approval, more anxious than before. He's gone, Epictetus says, into a finer, fatter slavery.
The turn: freedom isn't won by getting everything you desire, but by removing the desire, the craving for what isn't yours to control.
What's left is wanting what is in your own power, and holding the rest loosely. That isn't wanting nothing. It's wanting well.
A person who wants to be honest today can be. A person who wants everyone to like them is at the mercy of everyone. Same person, same day.

how: Stoic practice often means sorting a desire into the part that depends on oneself and the part that doesn't, and putting one's effort and hope on the first part.

o: freedom: doing whatever you like, no rules
freedom: rising so high no one can rule you
freedom: wanting only what's in your power

games.q: free is wanting rightly — tap the pairs.

s: for Epictetus, freedom comes from getting everything you desire
he says it comes from removing the desire for what isn't in your power.
Epictetus says no one wishes to live deceived or unjust
so anyone living that way isn't living as they wish, and by his definition isn't free.
in his story, the freed slave finally finds peace in the senate
at every rung he's serving someone; Epictetus calls it a finer slavery.

games.q: you've just been freed. you have nothing, and a rich man offers you dinner every night if you'll flatter him. what does Epictetus' freed slave do?
o: takes the deal, and keeps climbing.
goes back to his old master.
games.why: in the story he flatters, climbs, gets rich, even reaches the senate, and is never free, because his wants still belong to other people.

practice: Think of one thing you want badly right now, a reply, a raise, someone's approval, and ask the Stoic question: which part of this is in my power? Maybe not the raise, but excellent work; not their reply, but how kindly you wrote.
Let the want slide onto that part, and breathe with the smaller, steadier want.

wordCard.voice: Eleutheria. Greek for freedom: Epictetus' claim, On Freedom, that the free person lives as they wish, and the only way to do that is to wish for what is truly in their power.

orig.note: Greek: freedom; the subject of Discourses 4.1, Peri eleutherias, On Freedom.
